name: Annex 22 in the Plant
blurb: What the draft EU AI annex asks of manufacturers.
title: Annex 22 in the Plant
answer: Draft Annex 22 applies to AI models used in critical GMP applications. It expects a defined intended use, test data kept separate from training data, acceptance criteria set before testing, explainability where needed, and human review of outputs when the model is not fully reliable. It favours models that do not change once in use.

reading.body:
Draft Annex 22 would require AI models in critical GMP applications to have a defined intended use, independent test data, pre-set acceptance criteria, explainability where needed, and human review when the model is not fully reliable.

The pattern is procedural rather than technical. The annex does not name architectures or vendors. It asks for evidence that a model was specified before it was tested, that the test set was never seen during training, and that a human stays in the loop wherever the model cannot be trusted on its own. It also favours models that do not change once in use, which puts it at odds with the way most modern AI is built and updated.

For AI specifically, this matters because it shifts the burden from model capability to model control. A frozen model with a documented intended use is easier to accept than a more accurate one that drifts. That constrains where continuous learning and frequent retraining can be deployed in a plant, and it pushes validation work earlier, into how the model is scoped and how its data is partitioned.

The data covers only the draft text and its consultation date of 7 July 2025. It does not say whether the annex was finalised, what comments were received, or how any of this is enforced. It also does not connect the requirements to compute, power, or physical infrastructure, and nothing here supports a claim about them.

explainer:
In the plant, Annex 22 changes how an AI project is set up from day one. Before building, the team writes down the model's intended use, the inputs it will receive, the decision it supports and the people who will rely on it, with process experts involved. Acceptance criteria, such as minimum detection rates and maximum false rejects, are agreed before any testing.

Test data are kept separate from training data and chosen to represent real production, including rare defects and normal variation. The model is tested, documented and released under change control, then monitored in operation so drift is caught. Where the model is not fully reliable, a person reviews its output. Critical applications use models that are locked and give consistent outputs. Existing validation teams already know most of this discipline; the new elements are data independence, predefined performance criteria for statistical models, and monitoring.
